why_use_this:
Reach for this package when you need to numerically solve one of the three classical PDE types on a regular grid -- Laplace/Poisson (steady-state heat/potential, elliptic), the heat/diffusion equation (parabolic, time-marching), or the wave equation (hyperbolic, time-marching) -- and a closed-form solution either doesn't exist or isn't what you need (a discretized grid of values is). This is finite differences on a grid, not a general-purpose ODE integrator ([vani-calculus](https://github.com/enthusiasticgeek/vani-calculus)'s solvers step a single scalar state; PDE time-marching advances a whole grid per step, a different shape of problem entirely -- see the README's "Design decisions" for why this package deliberately doesn't depend on vani-calculus despite the surface similarity). Boundary conditions are Dirichlet-only for the elliptic solvers (fixed value at the border); the heat solvers additionally offer Neumann (fixed flux) and periodic (wraparound) variants. Before calling any `_step`/`_solve` function on the parabolic or hyperbolic side, check the matching stability number (`pde_heat1d_stability_r`, `pde_wave1d_courant`, etc.) yourself -- these explicit schemes are only conditionally stable and this package computes the number for you but does not enforce it.

Two running examples thread through the notes below: a 5-point grid \((i=0,\ldots,4)\) used for both the heat and wave equations, and the exact-linear-solution setup used for the Laplace solvers.

pde_laplace1d_assemble.intuition: The second derivative \(u''(x)\) measures curvature -- how much the slope itself is changing. On a discrete grid there's no true derivative to take, so we approximate curvature at point \(i\) by comparing it to the AVERAGE of its two neighbors: if \(u_i\) is exactly the average of \(u_{i-1}\) and \(u_{i+1}\), the curve is locally straight (zero curvature) there. This function builds a matrix that computes exactly that comparison, for every interior point at once.
pde_laplace1d_assemble.formula: \[ u''(x_i) \approx \dfrac{u_{i-1}-2u_i+u_{i+1}}{\Delta x^2} \] assembled into a dense \(n\times n\) matrix, with boundary rows replaced by identity rows (so a boundary row just says "\(u_0=\text{given value}\)" directly).
pde_laplace1d_assemble.example: For a 5-point grid (\(n=5\), \(\Delta x=0.25\), domain \([0,1]\)), row 2 (an interior point) reads \(\dfrac{u_1-2u_2+u_3}{0.0625}\) -- so that row of the matrix has \(1/0.0625=16\) in column 1, \(-32\) in column 2, and \(16\) in column 3. Row 0 and row 4 (the boundary rows) are instead just \([1,0,0,0,0]\) and \([0,0,0,0,1]\) -- identity rows that force \(u_0\) and \(u_4\) to equal whatever boundary value is supplied, regardless of the stencil.
pde_laplace1d_assemble.why: Replacing the boundary rows with identity rows (rather than trying to apply the stencil AT the boundary, where a neighbor like \(u_{-1}\) doesn't exist) is what lets `pde_laplace1d_solve` hand the WHOLE system -- interior stencil rows and boundary rows together -- to one single `mat_solve` call, rather than needing separate logic for boundary vs. interior points.

pde_laplace1d_solve.intuition: Unlike the heat and wave equations below (which MARCH FORWARD in time, one step building on the last), Laplace/Poisson has no time dimension at all -- it describes a STEADY STATE, so the whole grid's values are found all at once by solving one linear system, the same way you'd solve any other system of simultaneous equations.
pde_laplace1d_solve.formula: Solves \(u''(x)=f(x)\) (Laplace's equation is the special case \(f\equiv0\)) with Dirichlet boundaries \(u(0)=\text{left\_bc}\), \(u(L)=\text{right\_bc}\), via `pde_laplace1d_assemble` + `mat_solve`.
pde_laplace1d_solve.example: Solve pure Laplace (\(f\equiv0\)) on \([0,1]\) with \(u(0)=0\), \(u(1)=1\). The true solution to \(u''=0\) with these boundary values is the straight line \(u(x)=x\) (the simplest function with zero curvature that hits both boundary values). On the 5-point grid (\(x=0,0.25,0.5,0.75,1\)), the exact answer is therefore \((0,\,0.25,\,0.5,\,0.75,\,1)\) -- and because the 3-point stencil is EXACT for any function that's linear or quadratic in \(x\) (not just approximately right), `pde_laplace1d_solve` reproduces these values to floating-point precision, not just approximately.
pde_laplace1d_solve.why: This exactness-for-quadratics property is genuinely useful for testing: this package's own correctness tests build harder cases (like \(x^2-y^2\) in 2D) specifically because the stencil is provably exact for them, giving a real ground truth to check the numeric solver against instead of only comparing against another approximation.

pde_laplace2d_assemble.intuition: The same curvature-vs-neighbor-average idea as `pde_laplace1d_assemble`, just checking BOTH the horizontal and vertical neighbors now instead of only left/right.
pde_laplace2d_assemble.formula: \[ \nabla^2u_{i,j} \approx \dfrac{u_{i-1,j}-2u_{i,j}+u_{i+1,j}}{\Delta x^2} + \dfrac{u_{i,j-1}-2u_{i,j}+u_{i,j+1}}{\Delta y^2} \] assembled into a dense \((n_xn_y)\times(n_xn_y)\) matrix, boundary rows again replaced by identity rows.
pde_laplace2d_assemble.example: This 5-point (in 2D: up/down/left/right/center) stencil is exact for a saddle-shaped quadratic like \(u(x,y)=x^2-y^2\): \(\partial^2u/\partial x^2=2\) and \(\partial^2u/\partial y^2=-2\) everywhere, so \(\nabla^2u=2+(-2)=0\) -- \(x^2-y^2\) genuinely satisfies Laplace's equation exactly, and this package's own tests use it as ground truth for exactly that reason.
pde_laplace2d_assemble.why: Testing against a function you can verify by hand (rather than only against another numerical approximation) is what makes this a real correctness check, not just a "looks plausible" check -- see `pde_laplace1d_solve`'s example for the 1D version of the same idea.

pde_laplace2d_solve.intuition: Same steady-state, solve-the-whole-grid-at-once idea as `pde_laplace1d_solve`, just with a bigger linear system (one unknown per 2D grid point instead of one per 1D grid point).
pde_laplace2d_solve.formula: Solves \(\nabla^2u=f\) with Dirichlet boundary values from `boundary`'s border entries, via `pde_laplace2d_assemble` + `mat_solve`.
pde_laplace2d_solve.example: Using \(u(x,y)=x^2-y^2\) (from `pde_laplace2d_assemble`'s example) as the exact solution with \(f\equiv0\): feeding this function's BOUNDARY values (its values on the border of whatever grid you choose) into `pde_laplace2d_solve` reproduces \(x^2-y^2\) at every interior point too, to floating-point precision -- the same exactness-for-quadratics property as the 1D case, now in 2D.
pde_laplace2d_solve.why: The linear system here has \(n_xn_y\) unknowns, so `mat_inv_n`/`mat_solve`'s \(O(n^3)\) cost grows as the CUBE of the total grid point count -- fine for the modest grid sizes this library targets, but a real practical limit if you tried to scale up to a very fine 2D grid (see the README's own note on this exact tradeoff).

pde_heat1d_stability_r.intuition: An explicit time-marching scheme like FTCS can "blow up" (produce wildly oscillating, meaningless numbers) if the time step is too large relative to the spatial grid spacing -- the stability number \(r\) tells you exactly where that danger line is.
pde_heat1d_stability_r.formula: \[ r = \dfrac{\alpha\,\Delta t}{\Delta x^2}, \qquad \text{stable only if } r\le0.5 \]
pde_heat1d_stability_r.example: With diffusion rate \(\alpha=1\), grid spacing \(\Delta x=1\), and time step \(\Delta t=0.5\): \(r = \dfrac{1\times0.5}{1^2}=0.5\) -- exactly at the stability boundary (this is the same \(\alpha,\Delta x,\Delta t\) used in `pde_heat1d_step`'s worked example below).
pde_heat1d_stability_r.why: Notice \(r\) shrinks as the SQUARE of \(\Delta x\) -- halving your grid spacing (to get more spatial resolution) forces you to shrink \(\Delta t\) by a factor of 4 to stay stable, not just 2. This quadratic cost is exactly why the implicit solvers (`backward_euler_step`-style methods, unconditionally stable regardless of step size) exist in [vani-calculus](https://github.com/enthusiasticgeek/vani-calculus) for stiff problems where this constraint becomes impractical.

pde_heat1d_step.intuition: At every interior grid point, look at how much higher or lower your two neighbors are on average compared to you, and move a fraction of the way toward that average -- exactly how heat actually flows: from hot spots toward cold spots, faster when the difference is bigger.
pde_heat1d_step.formula: \[ u_i^{n+1} = u_i^n + r\left(u_{i-1}^n - 2u_i^n + u_{i+1}^n\right), \qquad r=\alpha\Delta t/\Delta x^2 \]
pde_heat1d_step.example:
A 5-point grid (\(i=0,\ldots,4\)) with a "heat spike" initial condition \(u^0=(0,\,0,\,1,\,0,\,0)\) (all heat concentrated at the center point), fixed zero boundaries (\(u_0=u_4=0\)), and \(r=0.5\) (the maximum stable value, from `pde_heat1d_stability_r`'s example). Update each interior point:

\(u_1^1 = 0 + 0.5(u_0^0-2u_1^0+u_2^0) = 0+0.5(0-0+1)=0.5\).
\(u_2^1 = 1 + 0.5(u_1^0-2u_2^0+u_3^0) = 1+0.5(0-2+0)=1-1=0\).
\(u_3^1 = 0 + 0.5(u_2^0-2u_3^0+u_4^0) = 0+0.5(1-0+0)=0.5\).

New state: \(u^1=(0,\,0.5,\,0,\,0.5,\,0)\) -- the concentrated spike has spread OUTWARD to both neighbors and the center has dropped all the way to zero (an extreme, maximally-diffusive step since \(r\) is at its stability limit).
pde_heat1d_step.why: Notice the TOTAL heat isn't the same before and after (\(1\) before, \(0.5+0.5=1\) after -- actually conserved here, by coincidence of the symmetric spike), but the DISTRIBUTION has visibly spread out and flattened, exactly the qualitative behavior the heat equation is supposed to model. Running many more steps would keep flattening this toward a smooth bump and eventually toward all-zero, matching the fixed zero boundaries.

pde_heat1d_step_neumann.intuition: A Dirichlet boundary FIXES the value at the edge (like holding the end of a rod at a constant temperature); a Neumann boundary instead fixes the FLUX to zero (like wrapping the end of the rod in perfect insulation -- heat can't escape there, but the edge's own temperature is free to change). The trick to applying the same interior stencil at an insulated edge is to imagine a "mirror" point just outside the grid that always matches the point just inside it, so no net heat flows across the boundary.
pde_heat1d_step_neumann.formula: Same update as `pde_heat1d_step`, but using a reflected ghost point at each boundary: \(u_{-1}\equiv u_1\) at the left edge (and symmetrically, \(u_n\equiv u_{n-2}\) at the right), so the boundary point's own value is updated using its actual interior neighbor twice instead of a fixed value.
pde_heat1d_step_neumann.example: Reusing `pde_heat1d_step`'s spike example but with insulated (Neumann) boundaries instead of fixed zero ones: at the left edge (\(i=0\)), the ghost point \(u_{-1}\) is set equal to \(u_1^0=0\), so \(u_0^1 = u_0^0 + r(u_{-1}^0 - 2u_0^0+u_1^0) = 0+0.5(0-0+0)=0\) -- unchanged this particular step, since there was no heat near that edge yet. If heat later reaches the boundary, this reflection is what keeps it from leaking out.
pde_heat1d_step_neumann.why: This matters physically whenever a system is genuinely isolated at its boundary (a rod with insulated ends, a sealed container) rather than in contact with a fixed-temperature reservoir -- using Dirichlet boundaries by mistake on an insulated system would incorrectly let heat drain away at the edges.

pde_heat1d_step_periodic.intuition: A periodic boundary treats the grid as a RING instead of a line segment with two distinct ends -- point 0's left neighbor is point \(n-1\), wrapping around, and point \(n-1\)'s right neighbor is point 0. Useful for modeling something that's genuinely circular (heat around a ring-shaped object) or as a simplified stand-in for an infinite domain.
pde_heat1d_step_periodic.formula: Same FTCS update as `pde_heat1d_step`, but indices wrap around: \(u_0^{n+1} = u_0^n + r(u_{n-1}^n - 2u_0^n + u_1^n)\), and symmetrically at the other end.
pde_heat1d_step_periodic.example: Reusing `pde_heat1d_step`'s spike example \(u^0=(0,0,1,0,0)\) with periodic boundaries instead: \(u_0^1 = u_0^0 + 0.5(u_4^0 - 2u_0^0 + u_1^0) = 0+0.5(0-0+0)=0\) -- again unchanged this step, since the heat spike hasn't reached either edge of the ring yet. The difference from the fixed-zero or insulated versions would only show up once the spreading heat actually reaches index 0 or index 4 and starts wrapping around to affect the OTHER end.
pde_heat1d_step_periodic.why: Notice all three boundary variants (fixed, insulated, periodic) give IDENTICAL results this particular step, precisely because the spike started far from the boundary -- the boundary condition only starts to matter once whatever's diffusing actually reaches the edge, which is worth remembering when debugging "why don't my boundary conditions seem to do anything" for a short simulation.

pde_heat2d_stability_r.intuition: The same stability-boundary idea as `pde_heat1d_stability_r`, but now BOTH spatial directions contribute to how fast instability can creep in, so their contributions add together.
pde_heat2d_stability_r.formula: \[ r = \alpha\,\Delta t\left(\dfrac{1}{\Delta x^2}+\dfrac{1}{\Delta y^2}\right), \qquad \text{stable only if } r\le0.5 \]
pde_heat2d_stability_r.example: With \(\alpha=1\) and a SQUARE grid (\(\Delta x=\Delta y=1\)): \(r=\Delta t(1+1)=2\Delta t\). To stay at the stability limit \(r=0.5\), you'd need \(\Delta t=0.25\) here -- HALF the \(\Delta t=0.5\) the 1D case allowed with the same \(\alpha,\Delta x\), because the second spatial direction adds its own contribution to the instability risk.
pde_heat2d_stability_r.why: This is why 2D (and 3D) explicit heat/diffusion simulations need noticeably smaller time steps than the 1D case for the same spatial resolution -- each additional dimension tightens the stability constraint further.

pde_heat2d_step.intuition: Exactly `pde_heat1d_step`'s neighbor-averaging idea, just averaging against FOUR neighbors (up, down, left, right) instead of two.
pde_heat2d_step.formula: One explicit FTCS step applying the 5-point Laplacian stencil (from `pde_laplace2d_assemble`) times \(\Delta t\) to every interior grid point, with Dirichlet boundary values from `boundary` re-imposed after the update.
pde_heat2d_step.example: For a point surrounded by four neighbors all at value 1 while it itself sits at value 0 (a "cold spot" surrounded by "hot" neighbors), with \(r=0.5/4=0.125\) per direction summed to \(r=0.5\) total (so the stability bound from `pde_heat2d_stability_r` is respected): the update pulls this point roughly halfway toward its neighbors' average, the same qualitative "flow from hot to cold" behavior as the 1D case, just pulling from four directions instead of two.
pde_heat2d_step.why: Because this reuses the exact same 5-point stencil `pde_laplace2d_assemble` builds (just applied as a time-step increment instead of assembled into a static matrix), any correctness confidence in the STEADY-STATE 2D Laplacian carries over directly to the TIME-MARCHING 2D heat equation -- it's the same spatial operator, used two different ways.

pde_wave1d_courant.intuition: For a wave to be simulated correctly, information (the wave's disturbance) can't be allowed to "outrun" the grid -- it can move at most one grid cell per time step, or the simulation misses part of what should have influenced each point. The Courant number measures exactly this: how many grid cells the physical wave speed \(c\) would cross in one time step.
pde_wave1d_courant.formula: \[ C = \dfrac{c\,\Delta t}{\Delta x}, \qquad \text{stable only if } C\le1 \]
pde_wave1d_courant.example: With wave speed \(c=1\), grid spacing \(\Delta x=1\), and time step \(\Delta t=1\): \(C=\dfrac{1\times1}{1}=1\) -- exactly at the stability limit (the same setup used in `pde_wave1d_first_step`/`pde_wave1d_step`'s examples below).
pde_wave1d_courant.why: \(C=1\) exactly is a genuinely special case for the 1D linear wave equation on a uniform grid: at this precise value the numerical scheme becomes EXACT (no numerical dispersion at all), which is why it's deliberately chosen for the worked examples below -- see `pde_wave1d_step`'s note for what that exactness looks like concretely.

pde_wave1d_first_step.intuition: The wave equation's standard update needs TWO previous time levels ("where was it, and where was it just before that") to know which direction things are moving -- but at the very start, there's only ONE known state, \(u^0\). This function bootstraps the missing second state using a short Taylor-series argument based on the given initial velocity.
pde_wave1d_first_step.example:
Same 5-point grid as `pde_heat1d_step`'s example, but now for the wave equation: initial displacement \(u^0=(0,0,1,0,0)\) (a spike), initial velocity \(v_0=(0,0,0,0,0)\) (starting at rest), \(C=1\) (from `pde_wave1d_courant`'s example). Since \(v_0\equiv0\), the velocity term drops out entirely:

\(u_1^1 = 0 + 0 + 0.5\times1\times(u_0^0-2u_1^0+u_2^0) = 0.5(0-0+1)=0.5\).
\(u_2^1 = 1 + 0 + 0.5(u_1^0-2u_2^0+u_3^0) = 1+0.5(0-2+0)=1-1=0\).
\(u_3^1 = 0+0+0.5(u_2^0-2u_3^0+u_4^0)=0.5(1-0+0)=0.5\).

So \(u^1=(0,\,0.5,\,0,\,0.5,\,0)\) -- the spike has split into two half-height bumps moving outward, with the center back at zero. (Boundaries stay fixed at 0.)
pde_wave1d_first_step.why: This split-in-two behavior is exactly what the true wave equation predicts for a point disturbance starting at rest: it separates into a left-moving and a right-moving pulse, each carrying half the original disturbance -- the numerical scheme is already showing genuinely wave-like behavior after just one step.

pde_wave1d_step.intuition: Once two previous states are known, the wave equation's central-difference update looks at how much a point moved from two steps ago to one step ago, then continues that same rate of change UNLESS its neighbors are pulling it back (the curvature term) -- this is Newton's second law in disguise: acceleration (the curvature) determines how the velocity changes.
pde_wave1d_step.example:
Continuing `pde_wave1d_first_step`'s example: \(u^0=(0,0,1,0,0)\), \(u^1=(0,0.5,0,0.5,0)\), \(C=1\). Compute \(u^2\) at each interior point:

\(u_1^2 = 2(0.5)-0+1\times(u_0^1-2u_1^1+u_2^1) = 1-0+(0-1+0)=1-1=0\).
\(u_2^2 = 2(0)-1+1\times(u_1^1-2u_2^1+u_3^1) = 0-1+(0.5-0+0.5)=-1+1=0\).
\(u_3^2 = 2(0.5)-0+1\times(u_2^1-2u_3^1+u_4^1) = 1-0+(0-1+0)=1-1=0\).

So \(u^2=(0,0,0,0,0)\) -- but this ISN'T the wave dying out; it's the two pulses from step 1 continuing to move outward past where this 5-point snapshot can see them (on a LARGER grid, you'd see the two half-height bumps still there, now one cell further out, at what would be positions \(-1\) and \(5\) relative to this small grid -- absorbed by the fixed boundary here since the grid is only 5 points wide).
pde_wave1d_step.why: At exactly \(C=1\), this scheme is provably EXACT for the 1D linear wave equation on a uniform grid (a special, well-known property of this specific stability boundary) -- the pulses move exactly one grid cell per time step with no spreading or distortion, unlike \(C<1\), where some numerical dispersion (a small amount of unwanted spreading) is unavoidable.

pde_wave2d_courant.intuition: The same "can't outrun the grid" idea as `pde_wave1d_courant`, with contributions from both spatial directions added the same way `pde_heat2d_stability_r` adds its two directions -- but under a SQUARE ROOT this time, not a plain sum.
pde_wave2d_courant.formula: \[ C = c\,\Delta t\sqrt{\dfrac{1}{\Delta x^2}+\dfrac{1}{\Delta y^2}}, \qquad \text{stable only if } C\le1 \]
pde_wave2d_courant.example: With \(c=1\) and a square grid \(\Delta x=\Delta y=1\): \(C = \Delta t\sqrt{1+1}=\Delta t\sqrt2\). To stay at \(C=1\), \(\Delta t\) must be \(1/\sqrt2\approx0.707\) here -- smaller than the 1D case's \(\Delta t=1\) for the same \(c,\Delta x\), the 2D wave equation's own tightened stability constraint.
pde_wave2d_courant.why: Because the bound involves a SQUARE ROOT of the summed direction-contributions (not a plain sum the way `pde_heat2d_stability_r` does), the 2D wave equation's stability constraint doesn't tighten as sharply as the heat equation's does when adding dimensions -- worth noticing the two stability formulas have genuinely different shapes, not just "the same idea with more terms."

pde_wave2d_step.intuition: Exactly `pde_wave1d_step`'s two-previous-states-plus-curvature idea, with the curvature term now summing contributions from all four neighboring directions (the 2D 5-point Laplacian) instead of just two.
pde_wave2d_step.example: A disturbance concentrated at one grid point (the 2D analog of `pde_wave1d_first_step`'s 1D spike) spreads outward as a genuinely 2D pattern under this update -- not just splitting into two pulses moving in opposite directions along one line, but spreading in a ring in every direction across the 2D grid, since the curvature term now pulls from four neighbors instead of two.
pde_wave2d_step.why: This is the discrete analog of a real 2D wave phenomenon -- ripples spreading outward from a point disturbance in a pond, in every direction at once, rather than just left/right along a line.
